title: Is It the Full Moon?
author: Paul Urry
summary: A headteacher takes the staffroom's favourite explanation for a chaotic day and tests it against the research, then does something more useful than debunking it. The lunar evidence collapses quickly: large psychiatric studies find nothing, and the biggest study of children, using more than thirty-three thousand days of accelerometer data across twelve countries, finds about five minutes less sleep around a full moon and no meaningful change in activity. Rather than concluding that teachers are simply wrong, Urry separates the observation from the explanation and argues the observation may be sound while the attribution is not. He then lines up the better candidates, namely heat, sleep, daylight and circadian timing, and air pollution, noting the irony that the environmental factor with the strongest evidence gets almost no staffroom discussion while the moon gets plenty. Wind gets an honest verdict of thin evidence, with the suggestion that what teachers notice on windy days is the sensory and logistical chaos wind causes rather than the air itself. The leadership payoff is a reframing of the first question after a difficult day, from what is wrong with the child to what changed around the child, plus a proposal that schools log incidents against environmental variables and test their own folklore.
points: Distinguishes a real observation from a wrong attribution, which lets the piece take teacher intuition seriously while discarding the lunar explanation.
Cites the accelerometer study of 5,812 children as the strongest available test, and notes its five-minute sleep difference is too small to explain anything teachers actually see.
Ranks heat, sleep, light and air quality above the moon on evidence, and flags air pollution as the best-supported factor nobody talks about.
Declines to confirm the windy-day belief, instead proposing that noise, banged doors and disrupted playtime supply the mechanism people credit to the wind.
Proposes a term-long, staff-blind log of incidents against weather and environment variables so a school can test its own folklore rather than argue about it.
quotes: Talk to teachers for long enough, and you will hear remarkably similar observations. Windy days are different. The first really hot day of the year is difficult.
Around a full moon, children slept approximately five minutes less per night than around a new moon.
If thousands of people working with children independently develop similar beliefs, it is worth asking what they are actually noticing.
A tired child hasn’t suddenly forgotten the behaviour policy.
But it is fascinating that one environmental influence for which we have reasonable evidence gets almost no attention in conversations about behaviour
We often talk about behaviour as though it resides entirely inside the child.
Once we believe something, we become very good at finding evidence for it.
